title: Readings From Somewhere Else: Parsing a Log You Did Not Write

questions.question: A log field contains 1,5 because it was written where the decimal separator is a comma. What does std::stod give you?
options: nan
1.5, since it understands both separators
It throws, because the field is malformed
1, silently, having used only the first character
questions.explanation: stod answers whether a field starts with a number, not whether it is one. Measured across seven fields it accepted all seven, including 1.5abc and 1.5.7. The decimal comma is the one that costs money: every reading in the file becomes a whole number and the result is believable.

questions.question: What single check separates 1.5 from 1,5 when parsing?
options: Whether strtod consumed the whole field, by comparing its end pointer against the end of the text
Whether the result is finite
Whether the field contains a comma
Catching the exception stod throws
questions.explanation: strtod sets a pointer to just past whatever it used, and comparing that against the end of the trimmed text is the entire test. stod throws only when the field does not begin with a number at all, so it never fires on any of the dangerous cases.

questions.question: Why reject nan and inf, when strtod parses them happily?
options: Because they are not valid C++ doubles
A sensor cannot read either, and one nan poisons every average computed from the file
Because strtod sets errno for them
There is no reason to: they should be kept
questions.explanation: They are spellings strtod accepts. Refusing them where the data comes in is much cheaper than finding one later in an average, which is lesson 01-08's territory.

questions.question: A three column log contains the row 0.4,1,70,2.45, a decimal comma written in a comma separated file. What happens when each field is checked?
options: The second field fails to parse
strtod reports ERANGE on the third field
The row is rejected because it has a comma in it
Nothing: it splits into four fields and every one of them is a valid number
questions.explanation: Which is why field checking is not enough. Measured on a log with three bad lines, one was caught by parsing a field and two were caught only by counting columns: this row, and a row cut short when the logger was killed.

questions.question: Why does read_log report unparsable and wrong_width as two separate counts?
options: So the caller can add them together
To make the report longer
They are different problems: unparsable fields suggest a sensor fault, wrong widths suggest a format or locale mismatch
Because wrong width rows are warnings rather than errors
questions.explanation: Reporting one number for both leaves the reader guessing which. A file consistently one column too wide is a file written with a decimal comma, and the fix is to read it with a different separator rather than to patch the rows.

questions.question: Why does read_log take a std::istream rather than a filename?
options: A test can hand it a string with no file and no cleanup, and a program can hand it an ifstream
Because opening files is slow
To avoid needing a path type that works on Windows
So it can read from a network socket
questions.explanation: Depend on the interface, not the device: the same idea as the replay sensor in 05-02 and the injectable clock in 03-05. A filename ties the parsing to the filesystem, and the awkward test cases are then the ones nobody writes.
